Here we specify our modeling algorithms for calibrating and summarizing
radiocarbon dates.

### Summed Probability Distribution

The SPD uses a uniform prior $\text{U}$ to obtain posteriors for each sample in
$\mathbf{M}$, which means in effect row-normalizing the matrix.

$$
\mathbf{\tilde{M}} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{M1})^{-1}\mathbf{M}
$$
In R:

```r
M_tilde <- M / rowSums(M)
```

Then we take the column means of that row-normalized matrix.

$$
\mathbf{\hat{v}} = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{\tilde{M}}^{\top}\mathbf{1}
$$
In R:

```r
v <- colMeans(M_tilde)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

#| eval: false
```


### Composite Kernel Density

There are a variety of KDE methods for summarizing C14 samples (e.g. Bronk
Ramsey 2017 and McLaughlin 2018), but we use the simplest possible approach
here, just sampling from each sample's posterior and then running KDE on those
samples, iterating this some number of times (500 by default). The final
estimate of the true density is just the column means.

### Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Model

This is roughly equivalent to the model proposed by Price et al (2021), but not
exactly the same. There are three notable changes. First, to specify the
number of mixture components, we find the posterior mode for different values
of K and select the one that minimizes BIC, computed from the mixture
likelihood at the mode. Second, we let the prior on the component standard
deviations adapt to the number of years in the interval. And third, to sample the posterior
distribution, we implement adaptive dual averaging Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in a
torch module, rather than using Stan. During burn-in, the sampler estimates a
dense mass matrix from the covariance of the draws, which accounts for the
strong correlations between parameters of overlapping components. Because
mixture posteriors are multimodal, sampling starts from the posterior mode of
the selected model, slightly jittered, rather than from a random point.

```{r}
#| label: bgmm
#| file: R/bgmm.R
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: R/bgmm.R
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| label: bgmm-example
#| time_it: true

```

### Dirichlet Process Mixture Model

We use the DPMM with Polya Urn sampling as recommended by Heaton in the
[`carbondate`
documentation](https://tjheaton.github.io/carbondate/reference/PolyaUrnBivarDirichlet.html):

> The library provides two slightly-different update schemes for the MCMC. In
> this particular function, updating of the DPMM is achieved by a Polya Urn
> approach (Neal 2000) This is our recommended updating approach based on
> testing.

Let $c_{i}$ hold the cluster assignment of each measurement $i = 1, ..., n$.
The $c_{i}$ are drawn using Polya Urn sampling

$$
c_{i} \mid t_{i}, \xi_{k}, n_{k} \sim \mathrm{Categorical}(r_{i1}, ..., r_{iK+1}), 
\qquad r_{ik} \propto 
\begin{cases}
  n_{k} \hspace{2pt} N(t_{i} \mid \mu_{k}, \tau_{k}^{-1}) 
    & \quad\text{existing cluster} k \\
  \alpha_{d} \hspace{2pt} T(t_{i} \mid \mu_{\phi}, \tau_{\phi}, 2\alpha) 
    & \quad\text{new cluster} K + 1
\end{cases}
$$

with $\xi_{k} = \{\mu_{k}, \tau_{k}\}$ being the mean and precision
($\tau = 1/\sigma^2$) of cluster $k$, $n_{k}$ the size of $k$ excluding $i$,
$r_{ik}$ the probability of sample $i$ being assigned to $k$, $\alpha_{d}$ the
concentration parameter of the Dirichlet Process, $T$ the location-scale
Student's t-distribution with $2\alpha$ degrees of freedom, $\mu_{\phi}$ a
hyper-parameter specifying the base mean for clusters, $\tau_{\phi}$ the base
precision of the new cluster t-distribution derived from the Normal-Gamma
described below. 

The Normal-Gamma serves as the joint prior for the means and precisions of the
mixture distribution

$$
\xi_{k} \mid \mu_{\phi} \sim 
\mathrm{NormalGamma}(\mu_{\phi}, \lambda, \alpha, \beta)
$$

with $\lambda$ a weight on the component errors. The shape and rate parameters
of the Gamma are updated each iteration based on the previous iteration's
calendar age estimates $\hat{t}_{i}$ and the current assignments $c_{i}$. As the
number of radiocarbon samples assigned to a cluster goes up, the shape parameter
increases, and with it the expected precision. Conversely, when the spread of
the calendar ages increases, the rate parameter also goes up, thereby decreasing
the expected precision. The precision is also penalized when the mean of the
cluster drifts from $\mu_{\phi}$.

Given the hard cluster assignments $c_{i}$, the conditional for the calendar
ages can use the Gaussians of the clusters as priors for age estimation, rather
than the full mixture density

$$
t_{i} \mid c_{i} = k, F_{i}, \xi_{k} \sim g_{ik}, 
\qquad
g_{ik}(t) \propto p(F_{i} \mid t) \hspace{2pt} N(t \mid \mu_{k}, \tau_{k}^{-1})
$$

Draws from this distribution are obtained using slice sampling (Neal 2003). So,
the Gibbs sampler assigns a scalar age estimate to each ^14^C date during each MCMC
iteration. Because cluster assignment happens during MCMC, radiocarbon samples
will wander across clusters in proportion to their likelihood. The individual
age estimates from each iteration are thus analogous to the mixture weighted
posterior age estimation method described above.

Gibbs sampling from these conditionals is implemented in performant C++ code in
the R package `carbondate`. The default number of MCMC iterations is 100,000,
but that proved impractical for the number of simulations given the resources of
a typical desktop computer, so we limit sampling to 50,000 iterations. The final
density estimate is the posterior predictive for the calendar age of a new
sample, obtained by averaging over a subset $s$ of Gibbs iterations,
$\hat{v} = 1/n_s \sum \hat{v}^{(s)}$, where each $\hat{v}^{(s)}$ is a mixture of
the occupied clusters, weighted by $n_k/(n + \alpha_d)$, plus a new-cluster
term, the Student-t above, weighted by $\alpha_d/(n + \alpha_d)$. Age estimates
are retained as draws from the posterior age distribution
$[\hat{t} \mid F, \theta]$ for each radiocarbon date, the per iteration sampled
ages.

### Gaussian Mixture Neural Network

NetC14 is a Gaussian Mixture Neural Network. To define that network, we first
implement torch modules for the model's forward pass and custom loss. We then
wrap these in a single model function that runs all the training logic,
including back-propagation.


The model forward pass is encapsulated in a module initialized with $K_{0} = \mathrm{min}(\mathrm{round}(\sqrt{m}), K_{max})$ 
clusters, where $K_{max}$ is the maximum number of allowed clusters (35 by 
default). Three length-$K_{0}$ vectors hold the log-transformed mixture 
parameters, with means initially spaced evenly across the interval. To construct
the mixture distribution, parameters must be transformed to satisfy certain 
constraints, including the same ordering constraint placed on means by the BGMM. 
The logits of the errors are exponentiated, ensuring that they are positive, and 
SparseMax is applied to the logits of the weights with a temperature $\pi$ 
controlling how aggressively the activation zeroes them out. The activation 
works by centering the logits around a threshold and then applying the rectified 
linear unit (ReLU) activation, with the threshold determined so that positive 
centered logits sum to one and the rest are set to zero 
(Martins and Astudillo 2016). Pruning components in this way rather than adding 
them satisfies the requirement imposed by neural networks that the dimensions of 
the data be known in advance. 

At initialization, the forward pass module embeds the Gaussian noise parameter 
$\xi$, the temperature $\pi$, and the counts of samples $n$ and years $m$. It 
then constructs the mixture distribution and evaluates the mixture over the 
annually-resolved grid interval $[t_{min}, t_{max}]$, returning an estimate of 
the density $\mathbf{\hat{v}}$. Tuning for the hyperparameters $\gamma$ and 
$\pi$ was done through a simple grid search over a range of values using the 
evaluation method described in the next section, resulting in default values
$\pi = 1.75$ and $\gamma = 2.5$. The model is trained over 512 epochs using the
Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.005 (Kingma and Ba 2017). Density estimates
$\mathbf{\hat{v}}$ are obtained by setting the model to training mode and
running multiple forward passes, generating unique estimates
$\mathbf{\hat{v}}^{(s)}$ with Gaussian noise that are then averaged,
$\mathbf{\hat{v}} = 1/n_{s} \sum \mathbf{\hat{v}}^{(s)}$, with the potential,
loosely speaking, to calculate confidence intervals, though they are not 
strictly probabilistic. Posterior age estimation is conducted in the manner 
described above.

